citations.quote:
Assume the smooth branch of the vacuum Maxwell postulate [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] on the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]: fields $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ jointly of class $C^1$ with the additional derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and continuous source densities $\rho,J$ of [[def-em-sources]]. Let $P,M$ and the derived objects $\rho_b,J_b,\rho_f,J_f,D,H$ be those of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]], with $P,M$ of class $C^2$, and use the operators of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. Then:

**(a) [Bound-source conservation]** $\partial_t\rho_b+\operatorname{div}J_b=0$ on $\Omega\times I$. Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the regular-distribution and classical-compatibility interfaces below. Identify continuous sources with their regular distributions using [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]] and [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]. Then

$$\partial_t\rho_f+\operatorname{div}J_f=\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J$$

as distributions on $U$, with derivatives as in [[def-distributional-derivative]]: the free pair is distributionally conserved exactly when the total pair is. Under the adopted four vacuum equations both sides are zero distributions, by [[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]]. These statements do not require classical derivatives of $\rho,J$. Where the partial derivatives $\partial_t\rho$ and $\partial_{x_i}J_i$ exist, the same identity holds pointwise by differentiating the free/bound decomposition; in particular, if these derivatives are continuous on $U$, both pairs satisfy the classical pointwise continuity equation. The bound-source conservation equation remains classical and uses only $P,M\in C^2$.

**(b) [Macroscopic equations]** On $\Omega\times I$,

$$\operatorname{div}D=\rho_f,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}H=J_f+\partial_tD.$$

**(c) [Interpretation and scope]** Equations (b) are an exact rewriting of the adopted vacuum equations under the decomposition of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]]: the two equations written in $E$ and $B$ are unchanged, and the $D$ and $H$ equations hold for every $C^2$ pair $(P,M)$, independently of any constitutive law. The classical bound identity of (a) uses the exchange of $\partial_t$ with $\operatorname{div}$ for $C^2$ data; the free/total identity is distributional in the stated continuous-source class, with its classical interpretation only under the additional derivatives stated in (a). The distributional conservation conclusion embeds the adopted smooth solution only; no macroscopic field-equation claim is made for the weak branch of the Maxwell postulate, for singular or sheet sources or for discontinuous $(P,M)$; no constitutive relation and no empirical statement is made.

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, its units, its fields $E,B$ and its source densities $\rho,J$ be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-si-conventions]], [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-sources]], and let the averaging convention be that of [[post-em-coarse-graining]], in whose sense the objects below are macroscopic. Any convolution used to instantiate that reading is taken on its declared exact interior-footprint domain, or under a declared locally integrable compatible extension covering every used footprint. Its every-time use requires every-time locally integrable spatial slices; joint spacetime local integrability alone supplies only the almost-every-time branch. The joint $C^2$ regularity specified below is a separate model hypothesis, not a consequence of spatial smoothing.

**(a) [Polarization and magnetization]** The material model specifies two maps $P,M:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] on the open set $\Omega\times I$: $P$ is the electric dipole moment per unit volume, in $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m^{-2}$, and $M$ the magnetic dipole moment per unit volume, in $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, both read in the frame basis. They are data of the chosen material model: this definition does not compute them from $E$ and $B$, and no relation between $(P,M)$ and the fields is asserted here.

**(b) [Bound sources]** Write $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ for the divergence and curl of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] taken at fixed $t$, and $\partial_t$ for the partial derivative of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] at fixed position, and define the bound charge density and bound current density by

$$\rho_b:=-\operatorname{div}P,\qquad J_b:=\partial_tP+\operatorname{curl}M.$$

Since $P,M$ are jointly $C^2$, $\rho_b$ and $J_b$ are continuous, indeed $C^1$, by the componentwise sum and product rules of [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]; $\rho_b$ carries $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m^{-3}$ and $J_b$ carries $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{-2}$.

**(c) [Free sources]** Define $\rho_f:=\rho-\rho_b$ and $J_f:=J-J_b$, in the same units as $\rho$ and $J$; these are the free charge and free current densities of the model. The decomposition $\rho=\rho_f+\rho_b$, $J=J_f+J_b$ is part of the chosen material model: the same total pair $(\rho,J)$ with a different pair $(P,M)$ is a different model.

**(d) [Displacement and magnetic intensity]** Define the electric displacement and the magnetic intensity by

$$D:=\varepsilon_0E+P,\qquad H:=\mu_0^{-1}B-M,$$

where $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and $\mu_0,c>0$ are the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; $D$ carries $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m^{-2}$ and $H$ carries $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{-1}$.

**(e) [Status]** This item fixes objects and the bound/free convention only. No field equation (the item `pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell`), no constitutive relation (the item `post-em-material-closure`), no conservation of the bound pair (the item `pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell`, clause (a)) and no identification of $P,M$ with microscopic dipole sums is asserted here.

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, its SI units and its fields $E,B$ be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-si-conventions]] and [[def-em-fields]]. Fix $a,b>0$, write $x_t=(x_1,x_2)$, $e_z:=e_3$, and define $\nabla_t f=(\partial_1f,\partial_2f,0)$, $\Delta_t f=\partial_1^2f+\partial_2^2f$ and $\operatorname{div}_tu_t=\partial_1u_1+\partial_2u_2$ for the stated regularity, using [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]].
(a) [Straight guide] A straight guide region is $\Omega_A:=A\times\mathbb R$ where $A$ is either a bounded connected $C^1$ plane domain ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]) or the explicit rectangular cross-section; the rectangle has corners and is treated by its open faces, not asserted to be a $C^1$ boundary domain, with longitudinal axis $e_z$; for a rectangular cross-section $A=R_{ab}:=(0,a)\times(0,b)$ the region is called the rectangular guide and its walls are the four open faces $\{x_1=0\},\{x_1=a\},\{x_2=0\},\{x_2=b\}$. A rectangular cavity region is $\Omega_c:=(0,a)\times(0,b)\times(0,d)$ for fixed $d>0$, with the six open faces as its walls. The separate smooth-cavity spectral branch uses an explicitly declared bounded $C^\infty$ domain in $\mathbb R^3$ with its smooth PEC boundary; it is not the rectangular reflection class. Spatial derivatives are taken at fixed $t$; the fields are defined on $\Omega\times I$ with the regularity declared by each theorem.
(b) [PEC boundary model] On every open wall (a wall minus its edges) the ideal perfectly conducting boundary model declares the two conditions $n\times E=0$ and $n\cdot B=0$, where $n$ is the outward unit normal of that wall ($-e_1,+e_1,-e_2,+e_2$ on the four rectangular walls, and $\pm e_j$ on the six cavity walls). Its physical reading is the ideal-conductor limit of the stationary interface conditions of [[pthm-em-material-stationary-jumps]]: with $E=B=0$ inside the ideal conductor the tangential electric field and the normal magnetic field vanish, while the surface-charge and surface-current readings $\sigma_f=-n\cdot D$ and $K_f=-n\times H$ for the filling-side traces (the wall normal points from the filling into the conductor, so the jump is $0$ minus the filling trace) are determined by the traces and are not prescribed here. The supplier's hypotheses (a compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface with one-sided $C^1$ fields) cover a smooth stationary interface, not the $\sigma\to\infty$ idealization nor the box edges; the guide/cavity conditions on the open walls are therefore declared as an idealization of this definition, and no pointwise statement on the edges is made.
(c) [Zero-normal-B reflection class] For the rectangular box $Q=\prod_{j=1}^3(0,L_j)$ with $L=(a,b,d)$, the reflection class is the class of locally integrable fields $E,B$ on $Q$ whose extensions to the rectangular torus $\prod_j\mathbb R/(2L_j\mathbb Z)$, defined by extending $E_1$ evenly across the $x_1$-walls and oddly across the $x_2$-, $x_3$-walls and cyclically for $E_2,E_3$, and extending $B_1$ oddly across $x_1$ and evenly across $x_2,x_3$ and cyclically for $B_2,B_3$, are $L^2$ fields, together with the distributional constraints that $\operatorname{div}E$ and $\operatorname{div}B$ vanish on the torus for the extensions. This is the declared weak PEC model used for the cavity initial-value problem; when the reflected extensions are continuous across the walls, their odd components vanish there, giving $n\times E=0$ and $n\cdot B=0$ on the open walls. Smoothness only inside $Q$ does not imply this extension continuity. Initial data not in this class (for example data with trapped normal $B$) are excluded, as are the general $H(\operatorname{curl})$ boundary classes, which are defined by the mathematical suppliers and are not identified here with the classical conditions.
(d) [TE, TM, TEM] For a guide or cavity field $(E,B)$, the longitudinal components are $E_z:=E\cdot e_z$ and $B_z:=B\cdot e_z$; the field is called TE (transverse electric) if $E_z\equiv0$, TM (transverse magnetic) if $B_z\equiv0$, and TEM if both vanish, always relative to the named axis $e_z$.
(e) [Separated phasor convention] For $\omega>0$ and $\beta\in\mathbb C$, a $\beta$-$\omega$ separated phasor field on the guide is a real field of the form $F(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\tilde F(x_1,x_2)e^{i(\beta x_3-\omega t)}\bigr)$ with a complex amplitude $\tilde F$, componentwise; $\omega/(2\pi)$ is the frequency and $\beta$ the longitudinal propagation constant; when $\beta$ is real, $\beta>0$ describes propagation in the $+e_z$ direction under this phase convention, while a complex $\beta$ gives the spatial factor $e^{-\operatorname{Im}\beta x_3}$ and may grow in the opposite direction; each consuming branch states its selection.
(f) [Scope] The definition fixes the geometry, the PEC boundary model, the weak reflection class and the mode terminology; it asserts no field equation, no constitutive law and no existence or completeness of modes, Rectangular TE/TM candidates and the rectangular reflection class, declared smooth bounded PEC cavity spectral classes, and smooth straight-guide TEM potential branches (including the coaxial annulus) are within this geometry. No general non-rectangular TE/TM guide theory, circular-guide spectral classification, open-end or junction scattering, or arbitrary lossy model is supplied. The same stationary PEC geometry also hosts the explicitly declared constant scalar Ohmic cavity class and the full longitudinal finite-energy reflection class of the straight rectangular guide; constitutive and evolution claims belong to their consuming theorems, not this definition.

**Conventions fixed by this definition.** The definition records objects and conditions only: the guide and cavity regions, their open walls and outward normals, the ideal PEC boundary conditions with their interface reading and excluded idealization, the zero-normal-$B$ reflection class with its distributional divergence constraints, the axis-relative TE/TM/TEM terminology, and the separated phasor encoding of real fields. It asserts no field equation, no constitutive relation, no existence, uniqueness or completeness of modes, and no dissipation or energy claim; those belong to the consuming theorems, each of which restates the branch of the material model it uses. The rectangular cross-section is treated through its four open faces and is not asserted to be a $C^1$ boundary domain, and no pointwise condition on box edges is made.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

**(b) [Elementary inertial-rest branch]** In the rest frame, with constant symmetric positive-definite matrices $\varepsilon,\mu\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ (the isotropic scalar cases $\varepsilon=\varepsilon\mathbf 1$, $\mu=\mu\mathbf 1$ with $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ included), the model takes

$$D=\varepsilon E,\qquad B=\mu H,\qquad J_c=\sigma E,$$

where $\sigma\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ is symmetric positive semidefinite and $J_c$ is the conduction part of the free current, $J_f=J_c+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ for a declared external free current $J_{\mathrm{ext}}:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ in $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. For a real matrix $T$, symmetric means $T^{\mathsf T}=T$, positive definite means $v^{\mathsf T}Tv>0$ for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^3$, and positive semidefinite means $v^{\mathsf T}Tv\ge0$ for every $v$. Entries of $\varepsilon,\mu,\sigma$ carry respectively $\mathrm F\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, $\mathrm H\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $\mathrm S\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, where $\mathrm F=\mathrm C/\mathrm V$, $\mathrm H=\mathrm T\,\mathrm m^2/\mathrm A$ and $\mathrm S=\mathrm A/\mathrm V$; these make the three displayed relations dimensionally consistent. Local, linear and nondispersive (instantaneous) response is part of this restricted assumption. In the isotropic case an exact broadband interpretation of the constant-coefficient law additionally requires $\varepsilon\mu\ge c^{-2}$, so that the characteristic speed $1/\sqrt{\varepsilon\mu}$ does not exceed the vacuum speed $c$; without that condition, and in the anisotropic branch, the constant-coefficient law is a declared finite-band effective phase-response model and carries no universal front-speed claim.

Assume the elementary inertial-rest branch of [[post-em-material-closure]]: constant symmetric positive-definite matrices $\varepsilon,\mu\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ (isotropic scalar case included) with $D=\varepsilon E$ and $B=\mu H$, and the conduction relation $J_f=\sigma E+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ with $\sigma$ symmetric positive semidefinite and a declared external free current $J_{\mathrm{ext}}$. Assume the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with the regularity hypotheses of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]], so that its macroscopic equations hold on $\Omega\times I$. Define the stored-energy density and the energy-flux vector

$$u:=\tfrac12\bigl(E\cdot D+B\cdot H\bigr),\qquad S:=E\times H,$$

with the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]; $u$ carries $\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-1}\mathrm s^{-2}$ and $S$ carries $\mathrm W\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. Then:

**(a) [Local balance and positivity]** On $\Omega\times I$,

$$\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S=-J_f\cdot E.$$

Moreover $u=\tfrac12(E\cdot\varepsilon E+H\cdot\mu H)\ge0$, with $u(x,t)>0$ whenever $(E(x,t),H(x,t))\ne(0,0)$.

**(b) [Dissipation reading]** With $J_f=\sigma E+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ and $\sigma$ symmetric positive semidefinite, $E\cdot\sigma E\ge0$ and the balance reads

$$\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S+E\cdot\sigma E=-J_{\mathrm{ext}}\cdot E;$$

the nonnegative term $E\cdot\sigma E$ is the Ohmic dissipation density of the model.

**(c) [Fixed-volume balance]** Let $\Omega'\subseteq\Omega$ be open with $\overline{\Omega'}\subseteq\Omega$ carrying the finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation of [[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]], let $t_0<t_1$ with $(t_0,t_1)\subseteq I$, assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) as in that divergence theorem, and let $n$ be the outward unit normal of $\partial\Omega'$. Then for every $t\in(t_0,t_1)$,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega'}u(x,t)\,dx=-\int_{\Omega'}J_f\cdot E\,dx-\oint_{\partial\Omega'}S\cdot n\,dS.$$

**(d) [Scope]** The density $u=\tfrac12(E\cdot D+B\cdot H)$ is a stored-energy density only for this constant symmetric nondispersive model; for general dispersive, nonlocal, nonlinear or hysteretic response no instantaneous stored-energy density is defined or claimed by this item, and the general dispersive work balance is not supplied. The identities hold only where the fields and sources have the stated regularity, the fixed-volume form keeps its boundary term, and conservation of $\int_{\Omega\prime}u$ requires the sum of outward flux and volume work on the right of (c) to vanish, not merely zero boundary flux. No empirical claim is made.

**(b) [Elementary inertial-rest branch]** In the rest frame, with constant symmetric positive-definite matrices $\varepsilon,\mu\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ (the isotropic scalar cases $\varepsilon=\varepsilon\mathbf 1$, $\mu=\mu\mathbf 1$ with $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ included), the model takes

$$D=\varepsilon E,\qquad B=\mu H,\qquad J_c=\sigma E,$$

where $\sigma\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ is symmetric positive semidefinite and $J_c$ is the conduction part of the free current, $J_f=J_c+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ for a declared external free current $J_{\mathrm{ext}}:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ in $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. For a real matrix $T$, symmetric means $T^{\mathsf T}=T$, positive definite means $v^{\mathsf T}Tv>0$ for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^3$, and positive semidefinite means $v^{\mathsf T}Tv\ge0$ for every $v$. Entries of $\varepsilon,\mu,\sigma$ carry respectively $\mathrm F\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, $\mathrm H\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $\mathrm S\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, where $\mathrm F=\mathrm C/\mathrm V$, $\mathrm H=\mathrm T\,\mathrm m^2/\mathrm A$ and $\mathrm S=\mathrm A/\mathrm V$; these make the three displayed relations dimensionally consistent. Local, linear and nondispersive (instantaneous) response is part of this restricted assumption. In the isotropic case an exact broadband interpretation of the constant-coefficient law additionally requires $\varepsilon\mu\ge c^{-2}$, so that the characteristic speed $1/\sqrt{\varepsilon\mu}$ does not exceed the vacuum speed $c$; without that condition, and in the anisotropic branch, the constant-coefficient law is a declared finite-band effective phase-response model and carries no universal front-speed claim.

Assume the smooth branch of the vacuum Maxwell postulate [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] on the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]: fields $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ jointly of class $C^1$ with the additional derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and continuous source densities $\rho,J$ of [[def-em-sources]]. Let $P,M$ and the derived objects $\rho_b,J_b,\rho_f,J_f,D,H$ be those of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]], with $P,M$ of class $C^2$, and use the operators of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. Then:

**(a) [Bound-source conservation]** $\partial_t\rho_b+\operatorname{div}J_b=0$ on $\Omega\times I$. Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the regular-distribution and classical-compatibility interfaces below. Identify continuous sources with their regular distributions using [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]] and [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]. Then

$$\partial_t\rho_f+\operatorname{div}J_f=\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J$$

as distributions on $U$, with derivatives as in [[def-distributional-derivative]]: the free pair is distributionally conserved exactly when the total pair is. Under the adopted four vacuum equations both sides are zero distributions, by [[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]]. These statements do not require classical derivatives of $\rho,J$. Where the partial derivatives $\partial_t\rho$ and $\partial_{x_i}J_i$ exist, the same identity holds pointwise by differentiating the free/bound decomposition; in particular, if these derivatives are continuous on $U$, both pairs satisfy the classical pointwise continuity equation. The bound-source conservation equation remains classical and uses only $P,M\in C^2$.

**(b) [Macroscopic equations]** On $\Omega\times I$,

$$\operatorname{div}D=\rho_f,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}H=J_f+\partial_tD.$$

**(c) [Interpretation and scope]** Equations (b) are an exact rewriting of the adopted vacuum equations under the decomposition of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]]: the two equations written in $E$ and $B$ are unchanged, and the $D$ and $H$ equations hold for every $C^2$ pair $(P,M)$, independently of any constitutive law. The classical bound identity of (a) uses the exchange of $\partial_t$ with $\operatorname{div}$ for $C^2$ data; the free/total identity is distributional in the stated continuous-source class, with its classical interpretation only under the additional derivatives stated in (a). The distributional conservation conclusion embeds the adopted smooth solution only; no macroscopic field-equation claim is made for the weak branch of the Maxwell postulate, for singular or sheet sources or for discontinuous $(P,M)$; no constitutive relation and no empirical statement is made.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $Q=\prod_{j=1}^3(0,L_j)$ with $L_j>0$ and let $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ be constants. Define the reflection boundary class by extending $E_1$ evenly across the $x_1$-walls and oddly across the $x_2,x_3$-walls, and cyclically for $E_2,E_3$; extend $B_1$ oddly across $x_1$ and evenly across $x_2,x_3$, cyclically for $B_2,B_3$. Work on the rectangular torus $\prod_j\mathbb R/(2L_j\mathbb Z)$ in the real $L^2$ fields with these parities and distributional $\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{div}B=0$. For smooth fields the parity class gives $n\times E=0$ and $n\cdot B=0$ on $\partial Q$. Then: (i) the finite separated Fourier modes are dense in this class, and the class is complete for the $L^2$ pairing ([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]], [[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]); (ii) for every initial datum in the class there is a unique $C(\mathbb R;L^2)$ weak solution of $\partial_tE=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1}\operatorname{curl}B$, $\partial_tB=-\operatorname{curl}E$ in the same class ([[def-distributional-derivative]]); (iii) the energy $\tfrac12\int_Q(\varepsilon|E|^2+|B|^2/\mu)\,dx$ is constant along the solution. This is an explicit weak PEC model; it supplies neither trace regularity for arbitrary $H(\operatorname{curl})$ fields nor completeness in lossy, open or non-rectangular guides.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, as used by the complete variational, Sobolev-extension and compact-spectral suppliers. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^\infty$ domain. Define $H(\operatorname{curl})=\{u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\operatorname{curl}u\in L^2\}$ and $H(\operatorname{div})=\{u\in L^2:\operatorname{div}u\in L^2\}$ with their graph norms, and let $X$ be the graph-norm closure in $H(\operatorname{curl})\cap H(\operatorname{div})$ of the smooth fields on the closure with $n\times u=0$; this is an explicit weak perfect-electric-conductor boundary class. Put $V=\{u\in X:\operatorname{div}u=0\}$ and $H=\overline{V}^{\,L^2}$. Then the curl form on $V$ has a complete orthonormal $L^2$ eigenbasis with nonnegative eigenvalues $\lambda_j$ of finite multiplicity tending to infinity whenever $H$ is infinite dimensional, and the zero eigenspace is finite dimensional and must be retained when the topology allows it. Each eigenfield $u_j\in V$ satisfies the full graph-class variational identity $\int_\Omega\operatorname{curl}u_j\cdot\operatorname{curl}v=\lambda_j\int_\Omega u_j\cdot v$ for every $v\in X$. The eigen equation is $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}u_j=\lambda_ju_j$ distributionally with the PEC trace, and for every explicitly chosen mathematical speed $v_{\mathrm{wave}}>0$ and every initial displacement $q_0\in V$ and velocity $q_1\in H$, the associated second-order wave has coefficients $a_j''+v_{\mathrm{wave}}^2\lambda_ja_j=0$ with those initial coefficients. Its displacement lies in $C(\mathbb R;V)$ and its velocity in $C(\mathbb R;H)$; finite modal sums converge respectively in $C(K;V)$ and $C(K;H)$ on every compact time interval $K$. The finite-dimensional $\lambda=0$ sector is retained with $a_j(t)=a_j(0)+ta_j'(0)$. This speed is a positive abstract mathematical parameter, not a physical constant or prerequisite. No identification with every maximal tangential-trace realisation, and no lossy, open or non-smooth-domain spectral claim, is made.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^\infty$ domain in the local graph sense of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], with outward Euclidean unit normal field $\nu$ on $\partial\Omega$. Restate the class conventions of [[lem-em-smooth-pec-cavity-spectral-closure]]: $L^2:=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ is the real Hilbert space of square integrable vector fields with the inner product $\langle u,v\rangle=\int_\Omega u\cdot v\,dx$ induced by the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and
$$H(\operatorname{curl})=\{u\in L^2:\operatorname{curl}u\in L^2\},\qquad H(\operatorname{div})=\{u\in L^2:\operatorname{div}u\in L^2\}$$
are the graph spaces with norms $\|u\|^2_{H(\operatorname{curl})}=\|u\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_2^2$ and $\|u\|^2_{H(\operatorname{div})}=\|u\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{div}u\|_2^2$, the curl and divergence being taken in the distributional sense; $X$ is the graph-norm closure in $H(\operatorname{curl})\cap H(\operatorname{div})$ of the fields that are smooth on a neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$ and satisfy $\nu\times u=0$ pointwise on $\partial\Omega$; and $V=\{u\in X:\operatorname{div}u=0\}$, $H=\overline V^{\,L^2}$. This is the explicit weak perfect-electric-conductor class of that item, not an identification with every maximal tangential-trace realisation.

Then:

(a) **Smooth PEC cavity.** The curl form $(u,v)\mapsto\int_\Omega\operatorname{curl}u\cdot\operatorname{curl}v$ on $V$ has a complete orthonormal $L^2$ eigenbasis $\{u_j\}$ with nonnegative eigenvalues $\lambda_j$ of finite multiplicity, with $\lambda_j\to\infty$ whenever $H$ is infinite dimensional and with the finite-dimensional zero eigenspace retained. Each eigenfield $u_j\in V$ satisfies $\int_\Omega\operatorname{curl}u_j\cdot\operatorname{curl}v=\lambda_j\int_\Omega u_j\cdot v$ for every $v\in X$; the eigen-equation $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}u_j=\lambda_ju_j$ holds distributionally together with the PEC trace; and $u_j$ has a $C^\infty$ representative on $\overline\Omega$ for which $\operatorname{div}u_j=0$, $\nu\times u_j=0$ and $\partial_\nu u_{j,n}+(\operatorname{div}\nu)u_{j,n}=0$ hold classically on $\partial\Omega$, where $u_{j,n}=u_j\cdot\nu$ and $\nu$ is extended constant along collar normal lines. For every explicitly chosen positive mathematical speed $v_{\mathrm{wave}}>0$ and every pair of data $q_0\in V$, $q_1\in H$, the associated second-order wave has coefficients solving $a_j''+v_{\mathrm{wave}}^2\lambda_ja_j=0$ with $a_j(0)=\langle q_0,u_j\rangle$ and $a_j'(0)=\langle q_1,u_j\rangle$, in the modal class of that item: its displacement lies in $C(\mathbb R;V)$ and its velocity in $C(\mathbb R;H)$, finite modal sums converge in $C(K;V)$ and $C(K;H)$ on every compact time interval $K$, and the finitely many $\lambda_j=0$ modes are $a_j(t)=a_j(0)+ta_j'(0)$. The speed is a positive abstract mathematical parameter and has no physical dependency. The scalar auxiliary Dirichlet resolvent used inside the recorded cavity argument has, for every $q\in L^2(\Omega)$, a unique solution $\varphi\in H_0^1(\Omega)\cap H^2(\Omega)$ of $(1-\Delta)\varphi=q$, with smooth zero-boundary approximants converging in $H^2$ and whose gradients converge in the PEC graph norm, by [[lem-em-dirichlet-resolvent-h-two-and-smooth-test-density]]. For smooth $q$ this solution is smooth on the closure by the same smooth-boundary bootstrap; no classical regularity for a general $L^2$ datum is asserted. Smooth unshifted scalar boundary problems have the classical upgrade of [[thm-em-elliptic-boundary-existence]] with $\varepsilon=I$.

(b) **Rectangular reflection-parity class.** Let $Q=\prod_{j=1}^3(0,L_j)$ with $L_j>0$ and let $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ be constants. In the reflection boundary class of [[lem-em-rectangular-pec-energy-completeness]] (real $L^2$ fields on the torus $\prod_j\mathbb R/(2L_j\mathbb Z)$ whose components carry the parities of that item and whose distributional divergences vanish), the finite separated Fourier modes are dense at every time, and every initial datum of the class has a unique $C(\mathbb R;L^2)$ weak solution of $\partial_tE=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1}\operatorname{curl}B$, $\partial_tB=-\operatorname{curl}E$ in the class, along which $\tfrac12\int_Q(\varepsilon|E|^2+|B|^2/\mu)\,dx$ is constant.

No completeness is asserted in lossy, open-ended or non-smooth classes, and the constant-Ohmic and open-longitudinal branches are homed separately as physical items on the guide page; they are not mathematical premises or dependencies of this statement.

The Euclidean inner product is that of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; at a boundary point with outward unit normal $
u$ the outward conormal vector is $\varepsilon

Edge and junction points, reentrant corners, coefficient loss of regularity and general piecewise classical regularity beyond finitely many disjoint smooth interfaces are excluded. The existence content of all three parts is that of the two weak solvability lemmas; this theorem states the combined existence-and-regularity conclusions on the declared domains and adds no existence assertion beyond them.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$. Then every $x\in H$ has a unique decomposition

$$x=m+n,\qquad m\in M,\quad n\in M^\perp ,$$

so that $H=M\oplus M^\perp$ as a direct sum of the subspace $M$ and its orthogonal complement.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be a complete orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert
space $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]) and
let $x\in H$, with partial sums
$P_Fx=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$ over finite $F\subseteq I$. Then:

1. $x$ is the norm limit of the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)$, that is
   $$x=\sum_{i\in I}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$$
   in the sense of convergence of the net of finite subsums;
2. **the coefficients are unique**: if $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ is a family in
   $\mathbb F$ whose finite-subset net $\sum_{i\in F}a_ie_i$ converges to $x$,
   then $a_i=\langle x,e_i\rangle$ for every $i\in I$;
3. the support $\{i : \langle x,e_i\rangle\ne0\}$ is at most countable, and the
   expansion does not depend on an ordering: if $(i_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ is a
   sequence of pairwise distinct elements of $I$ whose image contains the
   support, then the sequence of partial sums
   $\sum_{k<n}\langle x,e_{i_k}\rangle e_{i_k}$ also converges to $x$.

Claim 3 is the sense in which the expansion is **unconditional**: the sum is
independent of any ordering, because the finite-subset net converges and any
enumeration of a set containing the support by pairwise distinct indices is
cofinal in the squared mass.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Assume countable choice. On every measure space, complex $L^p$ is complete for $1\le p\le\infty$, and every norm-convergent sequence has a subsequence of measurable representatives converging a.e. to its limit. For finite $p$, finite simple functions with finite-measure support are dense, and on $\mathbb R^n$ with Lebesgue measure, $n\ge1$, complex $C_c^\infty$ is dense. Complex $L^2$ has the first-variable-linear inner product $\int f\overline g$, its norm is $\|\cdot\|_2$, and Cauchy–Schwarz has the following equality criterion: if $g\ne0$, equality iff $f=cg$ a.e.; if $g=0$, equality for all $f$. The finite-tuple version uses a common scalar across components.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

Distributional derivatives satisfy $\partial^\alpha\partial^\beta u=\partial^{\alpha+\beta}u$ and are continuous linear maps on $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ for both the weak and strong distribution topologies. These claims hold in ZF. Assuming Countable Choice for the cited Riemann-to-Lebesgue comparison, if $f\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ and $|\alpha|\le k$, then $\partial^\alpha u_f=u_{\partial^\alpha f}$. In particular distributional differentiation extends classical smooth differentiation.

Assume Countable Choice for the Lebesgue regular-distribution convention. If $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is nonempty, open and connected and $\partial_j u=0$ for every $1\le j\le n$, then there is a unique $c\in\mathbb C$ such that $u(\psi)=c\int\psi$ for every test. Conversely every constant regular distribution has zero first derivatives. On a disconnected open set constants may differ on different connected components.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $F:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and suppose one $L\ge0$ satisfies $\|F(t,x)-F(t,y)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2$ for all $t,x,y$. Then every IVP for $x'=F(t,x)$ has a unique global solution.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

$$\exp(x)\to+\infty\quad(x\to+\infty),\qquad \exp(x)\to0\quad(x\to-\infty),$$
and the range of $\exp$ is contained in $(0,\infty)$ and is unbounded above with infimum $0$.

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $F,G:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$. Then $F\times G$ is $C^1$ on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{div}(F\times G)=\langle\operatorname{curl}F,G\rangle-\langle F,\operatorname{curl}G\rangle,$$

$$\operatorname{curl}(F\times G)=(\operatorname{div}G)F-(\operatorname{div}F)G+DF\,G-DG\,F.$$

Here $DF\,G$ denotes the map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ whose $i$th coordinate at $p$ is $\sum_{j<3}\partial_jF_i(p)\,G_j(p)$, that is, the Jacobian matrix of $F$ at $p$ applied to the vector $G(p)$, and $DG\,F$ is defined the same way with the roles of $F$ and $G$ exchanged. The operators are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], the cross product is that of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], the inner product that of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and the Jacobian matrix that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $\phi:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$. Then $\nabla\phi$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{curl}\nabla\phi=0\qquad\text{on }U.$$

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. Both integrals are finite, with the continuous interior derivative convention and the outward normal on every boundary component.
For all $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $S\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be an embedded smooth submanifold. Then there is a
positive smooth function $\delta:S\to(0,\infty)$ such that the restricted
normal addition map
$$E:\Omega_\delta\to\mathbb R^m,\qquad \Omega_\delta:=\{(p,v)\in N^\perp S:\|v\|<\delta(p)\},$$
is a diffeomorphism onto an open neighbourhood of $S$. In particular, $S$ has a
tubular neighbourhood in $\mathbb R^m$.

Let $\beta$ be the standard flat function. The **standard smooth step function** is
$$ \sigma(t):=\frac{\beta(t)}{\beta(t)+\beta(1-t)}. $$
Because $\beta$ is smooth and positive on $(0,\infty)$, the denominator is positive on $(0,1)$, while $\sigma(t)=0$ for $t\le 0$ and $\sigma(t)=1$ for $t\ge 1$.

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

derivations.claim: [Rectangular damped modal system] Assume Countable Choice. Fix the box $Q$ and the reflection class of [F2], and let $(E,B)$ be a $C(\mathbb R;L^2)$ distributional solution of the damped first-order system of [F1] in that class. The finite separated Fourier modes are dense in the class by [F2], and for a wavevector $k\in(\pi/L_1)\mathbb Z\times(\pi/L_2)\mathbb Z\times(\pi/L_3)\mathbb Z$ the coefficient system of the damped system reads $\widehat E_t=iv^2\,k\times\widehat B-\gamma\widehat E$, $\widehat B_t=-ik\times\widehat E$: this is [F2]'s recorded coefficient system with the additional scalar term $-\gamma\widehat E$ of [F1], and the algebraic constraint $k\cdot(k\times w)=0$ preserves $k\cdot\widehat E=k\cdot\widehat B=0$, while the finite Fourier modes carry the parities of the class because the reflection rules are diagonal in the separated basis.

[Smooth PEC cavity spaces and the magnetic decomposition] Assume the full Axiom of Choice as in [F3], let $\Omega$ be a bounded $C^\infty$ domain and let $X,V,H$, $\{u_j\}$, $\lambda_j\ge0$ be the classes and eigenbasis of [F3]. Put $M:=\{B\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\int_\Omega B\cdot
abla\psi=0	ext{ for every smooth scalar }\psi	ext{ on }\overline\Omega\}$, the weak normal-zero divergence-free space, and $K_M:=\{B\in M:\operatorname{curl}B=0	ext{ distributionally}\}$. For each positive eigenvalue put $w_j:=\operatorname{curl}u_j/\sqrt{\lambda_j}$. Then the $w_j$ are orthonormal, $w_j\in M$, and $M=\overline{\operatorname{span}\{w_j:\lambda_j>0\}}^{L^2}\oplus K_M$. Orthonormality: the full-$X$ identity of [F3] with the test $v=u_l\in V\subseteq X$ gives $(\operatorname{curl}u_j,\operatorname{curl}u_l)=\lambda_j(u_j,u_l)=\lambda_j\delta_{jl}$, so $(w_j,w_l)=\delta_{jl}$. Membership and the forward inclusion: for a smooth scalar $\psi$, [F8] gives $\operatorname{div}(u_j	imes
abla\psi)=
abla\psi\cdot\operatorname{curl}u_j-u_j\cdot\operatorname{curl}
abla\psi=
abla\psi\cdot\operatorname{curl}u_j$, and its integral over $\Omega$ is the boundary integral $\int_{\partial\Omega}(n	imes u_j)\cdot
abla\psi=0$ because $u_j$ is smooth on the closure with $n	imes u_j=0$ [F3]; hence $w_j\in M$, and the closed span of the $w_j$ lies in $M$. For an element $u\in V$, the $V$-norm identity of [F3] with $\|u_j\|_V^2=1+\lambda_j$ gives the expansion $u=\sum_j(u,u_j)u_j$ in $L^2$, and applying the bounded operator $\operatorname{curl}$ on $V$ gives $\operatorname{curl}u=\sum_j(u,u_j)\sqrt{\lambda_j}w_j$ in $L^2$; hence $\overline{\operatorname{curl}V}=\overline{\operatorname{span}\{w_j\}}$, and both lie in the closed subspace $M$. Decomposition: the orthogonal decomposition theorem [F5] applied to the closed subspace $\overline{\operatorname{span}\{w_j\}}$ of $M$ writes $B\in M$ as the sum of its projections onto that span and onto its orthogonal complement inside $M$; it remains to identify the complement with $K_M$. If $B\in M$ is orthogonal to every $\operatorname{curl}v$ with $v\in V$ and $\varphi$ is smooth and compactly supported in $\Omega$, then the smooth Dirichlet solver [F4] with coefficient identity, zero boundary trace and source $-\operatorname{div}\varphi$ supplies a smooth $f$ on the closure with $\Delta f=\operatorname{div}\varphi$; then $\varphi-
abla f$ is smooth on the closure with $\operatorname{div}(\varphi-
abla f)=0$ and with vanishing tangential trace on $\partial\Omega$ (the first term is compactly supported, and $f|_{\partial\Omega}=0$ forces the tangential derivatives of $f$, hence $n	imes
abla f$, to vanish there), so $\varphi-
abla f$ lies in $V$; since $\operatorname{curl}(\varphi-
abla f)=\operatorname{curl}\varphi$ by [F8], we obtain $(B,\operatorname{curl}\varphi)=0$; as $\varphi$ is an arbitrary compactly supported smooth test, this is exactly the distributional statement $\operatorname{curl}B=0$, i.e. $B\in K_M$. Conversely, if $B\in K_M$ then for each eigenfield $u_j$ the collar cutoff of [F9] yields compactly supported smooth approximants $\eta_\delta u_j$ with $\eta_\delta u_j	o u_j$ and $\operatorname{curl}(\eta_\delta u_j)	o\operatorname{curl}u_j$ in $L^2$ (the boundary layer has width $2\delta$ and $n	imes u_j=0$ makes the boundary term vanish in the limit), so the distributional pairing $\int B\cdot\operatorname{curl}(\eta_\delta u_j)=0$ passes to the limit and gives $(B,\operatorname{curl}u_j)=0$, hence $(B,w_j)=0$; by continuity of the pairing and closedness of the span, $B$ is orthogonal to $\overline{\operatorname{span}\{w_j\}}$, which is the claimed complement and finishes the decomposition.

[Scalar characteristic classification] For parameters $\gamma\ge0$, $v>0$, $\lambda\ge0$, the solutions of $a''+\gamma a'+v^2\lambda a=0$ are classified by $\Delta:=\gamma^2/4-v^2\lambda$: if $\Delta>0$ the characteristic roots are $-\gamma/2\pm\sqrt\Delta$ and the general solution is $Ae^{(-\gamma/2+\sqrt\Delta)t}+Be^{(-\gamma/2-\sqrt\Delta)t}$; if $\Delta<0$ the roots are $-\gamma/2\pm i\sqrt{-\Delta}$ and the general solution is $e^{-\gamma t/2}(A\cos(\sqrt{-\Delta}t)+B\sin(\sqrt{-\Delta}t))$; if $\Delta=0$ it is $(A+Bt)e^{-\gamma t/2}$; and if $\lambda=0$ the solutions are $A+Be^{-\gamma t}$ for $\gamma>0$ and $A+Bt$ for $\gamma=0$. These are finite real computations with the square roots of [F7] and the real exponential and trigonometric solutions certified by [F7]; no choice principle is used.

[Rectangular class: global solutions, energy and convergence] For every initial pair in the rectangular class of [F2] the damped system of [F1] has a unique $C(\mathbb R;L^2)$ distributional solution in the class, finite Fourier mode sums converge in energy norm uniformly on compact time intervals and are dense at every time, and the coefficient equations of step 1.1 hold for every wavevector. Indeed, for each $k$ the right-hand side of the finite-dimensional system of step 1.1 is globally state-Lipschitz (it is affine), so [F7] gives a unique global solution through the initial coefficients; differentiate the per-mode energy $\varepsilon|\widehat E|^2+\mu^{-1}|\widehat B|^2$. With $C:=\overline{\widehat E}\cdot(k\times\widehat B)$ and $\overline{\widehat B}\cdot(k\times\widehat E)=-\overline C$, the curl contribution is $(2/\mu)\operatorname{Re}(iC+i\overline C)=0$ by the scalar triple-product identity of [F8] and complex conjugation [F9]; this gives $\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\varepsilon|\widehat E|^2+\mu^{-1}|\widehat B|^2\bigr)=-2\sigma|\widehat E|^2\le0$, so each modal energy is nonincreasing forward and bounded by $e^{2\gamma T}$ times its initial value on $[-T,T]$ (multiply by $e^{2\gamma t}$ and differentiate); Parseval for the complete class [F2] therefore controls the energy-norm of every omitted tail uniformly on compact times. Finite solutions converge in $C_tL^2$ to a limit in the class, and the linear distributional equations pass to the limit against compactly supported smooth periodic tests by Cauchy–Schwarz [F5] on a compact time support, exactly as in the lossless argument of [F2]; the constraints $k\cdot\widehat E=k\cdot\widehat B=0$ and the parities are preserved by step 1.1, so the limit lies in the same class. Uniqueness: a $C_tL^2$ weak solution has continuous coefficients whose distributional derivatives equal the displayed continuous right-hand sides; for each coefficient equation, subtract the oriented primitive of the continuous right-hand side, which is $C^1$ with that derivative by [F6], use the $C^1$ regular-distribution compatibility of [F6] to identify its distributional derivative, conclude that the difference has zero distributional derivative, hence is constant by [F6], and match the initial value; global uniqueness of the finite system identifies the coefficients, and completeness of the Fourier class identifies the fields.

[Smooth PEC cavity: modal system, variational equations and uniqueness] Assume the full Axiom of Choice as in [F3]. Let $H\times M$ be the energy class of steps 1.2, with $M=\overline{\operatorname{span}\{w_j\}}\oplus K_M$. For coefficients $a_j=(\cdot,u_j)$, $b_j=(\cdot,w_j)$ declare the first-order modal system $a_j'=v^2\sqrt{\lambda_j}\,b_j-\gamma a_j$, $b_j'=-\sqrt{\lambda_j}\,a_j$ for $\lambda_j>0$, and $a_j'=-\gamma a_j$ for the electric zero modes, and declare the magnetic kernel data constant, $(B,K_M)'=0$ for every kernel test. Endow the paired-magnetic space with the completion $D_M$ of finite $w_j$-sums plus $K_M$ for the norm $\|w\|_{D_M}^2:=\|w\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{curl}w\|_2^2$, and consider the weak variational equations $\langle E_t,\phi\rangle=v^2\langle B,\operatorname{curl}\phi\rangle-\gamma\langle E,\phi\rangle$ for $\phi\in V$ and $\langle B_t,\psi\rangle=-\langle E,\operatorname{curl}\psi\rangle$ for $\psi\in D_M$. Then every initial pair in $H\times M$ has a unique $C(\mathbb R;H\times M)$ solution of this declared realization, it satisfies the modal equations distributionally, and finite electric and paired-magnetic modal sums together with the static kernel component converge uniformly on compact time intervals in energy norm. Existence and uniqueness are finite-dimensional: each paired system is a globally Lipschitz constant-coefficient system solved by [F7], and the kernel data are constant, so a candidate solution is the norm-limit of its finite modal sums; the sums converge because the energy $\sum_j(\varepsilon|a_j|^2+\mu^{-1}|b_j|^2)$ is controlled as in step 2.1 and the kernel component is retained exactly. Each finite sum with the static kernel satisfies the first-order equations distributionally in the interior: $\operatorname{curl}w_j=\sqrt{\lambda_j}u_j$ follows from [F3], while the electric zero eigenfields and magnetic kernel have zero curl. Uniform compact-time $L^2$ convergence passes these linear equations to the limit against compactly supported smooth spacetime tests by Cauchy–Schwarz [F5]. For the variational equations, the finite sums satisfy them against finite spectral tests by the full-$X$ identity of [F3], and the density of the finite spectral tests in $V$ and in $D_M$ passes the identities to the limit by Cauchy–Schwarz [F5], since uniform energy convergence on compact times controls both pairings. Conversely, testing the variational equations against $u_j$ (for $\phi$) and $w_j$ or kernel vectors (for $\psi$) recovers the modal equations, so the weak realization and the modal system are equivalent in the stated class; uniqueness follows from the scalar ODE uniqueness and the complete decomposition of step 1.2. For strong first-order solutions with $E\in C^1_tH\cap C_tV$ and $B\in C^1_tL^2\cap C_tH(\operatorname{curl})$, the same pairing gives $a_j'=v^2(B,\operatorname{curl}u_j)-\gamma a_j$ and, differentiating with $B'=-\operatorname{curl}E$ and the full-$X$ identity, $a_j''+\gamma a_j'+v^2\lambda_j a_j=0$ with $a_j'=-\gamma a_j$ at $\lambda_j=0$. No maximal rough tangential-trace realisation is claimed.

[Exact energy balance] In both declared classes, for every $t_0<t_1$, $\mathcal U(t_1)+\sigma\int_{t_0}^{t_1}\|E(t)\|_2^2dt=\mathcal U(t_0)$ and $\mathcal U'(t)=-\sigma\|E(t)\|_2^2\le0$. In the rectangular class, sum the finite per-mode identities of step 2.1 over the wavevectors of a finite modal projection, integrate over $[t_0,t_1]$ with [F6], and pass to the limit using the uniform energy-norm convergence of step 2.1 to pass both the energy and the continuous $\|E(t)\|_2^2$-integral terms; in the smooth class, do the same with the paired modal energies of step 3.1 and the retained kernel component, whose curl vanishes. The derivative form then follows from the integral form by [F6]; the boundary term of a smooth local Poynting identity is not used, so no unprovided nonlinear weak local identity is asserted.

[Associated second-order branch] Independently of first-order compatibility, the same spectral basis gives the damped associated electric wave for every $q_0\in V$, $q_1\in H$, with $q\in C(\mathbb R;V)$, $q'\in C(\mathbb R;H)$ and modal convergence uniform on compact times: its coefficients satisfy $a_j''+\gamma a_j'+v^2\lambda_ja_j=0$ with prescribed initial coefficients $a_j(0)=(q_0,u_j)$, $a_j'(0)=(q_1,u_j)$, and at $\lambda_j=0$ they are $\alpha_j+\beta_j(1-e^{-\gamma t})/\gamma$ for $\gamma>0$ and $\alpha_j+t\beta_j$ for $\gamma=0$. Indeed, for $\lambda_j>0$ the function $Q_j=|a_j'|^2+v^2\lambda_j|a_j|^2$ satisfies $Q_j'=-2\gamma|a_j'|^2\le0$ by [F7], and the positive eigenvalues, being finite in multiplicity and tending to infinity, have a positive lower bound, so compact-time exponential bounds on $Q_j$ control the $V$ displacement and $H$ velocity tails by the weighted $V$-norm identity of [F3]; the finitely many zero modes have the displayed solutions by step 1.3, and the finite-sum FTC estimate of [F6] passes the $H$ derivative to the limit and identifies the variational second-order equation against compact-time tests. Such arbitrary second-order data need not arise from the first-order Maxwell system: its zero modes additionally satisfy $a_j'=-\gamma a_j$, and the broader wave is retained alongside the physical first-order branch. All square roots and real derivatives are those of [F7].

[Decay, zero sectors and long-time limits] For $\sigma>0$ (so $\gamma>0$) every positive mode decays: if $\Delta_j=\gamma^2/4-v^2\lambda_j>0$ the two real roots $-\gamma/2\pm\sqrt{\Delta_j}$ are negative; if $\Delta_j<0$ the complex roots have real part $-\gamma/2<0$, and the oscillatory factor is bounded by the cosine and sine identities of [F7]; if $\Delta_j=0$ the factor $t e^{-\gamma t/2}$ tends to zero by [F7]. The positive-mode derivatives $a_j'$ also tend to zero from the same explicit formulas, so $b_j=(a_j'+\gamma a_j)/(v^2\sqrt{\lambda_j})\to0$ for each positive mode. Electric zero modes obey $a_j(t)=a_j(0)e^{-\gamma t}$ by step 1.3, and magnetic kernel data stay constant by step 1.2, so in the smooth class the solution tends in energy norm as $t\to+\infty$ to $(0,P_{K_M}B(0))$, where $P_{K_M}$ is the orthogonal projection onto $K_M$ of step 1.2; the finite-head/finite-tail argument of step 3.1 passes the modewise convergence to the whole energy norm. For $\sigma=0$ the energy is constant by step 4.1, the electric zero modes are static by step 1.3 and the original lossless branch is recovered. The zero sectors are retained, not divided by their eigenvalues, and no universal decay to zero in the presence of magnetic kernel data is claimed.

[Scope] Clauses (a) and (b) are steps 2.1 and 3.1: the rectangular class has a unique finite-energy distributional solution with dense finite modes at every time, and the smooth PEC class has the declared weak realization with a unique solution and energy-norm convergence of finite modal sums; the decomposition of the magnetic space, including arbitrary kernel data, is step 1.2. Clause (c) is steps 4.1 and 5.1. Clause (d) is step 4.2. Clause (e): the argument used only the declared constant Ohmic branch, the ideal PEC boundary model, the finite-energy classes and the recorded spectral and elliptic suppliers; Countable Choice suffices for the rectangular branch, the smooth branch retains its full Choice premise, no arbitrary loss tensor, memory law, changing interface, open-end, rough-wall or empirical claim is made, and weak energy balance was proved by modal limits without asserting an unprovided nonlinear weak local Poynting theorem.
