Assume the smooth branch of the vacuum Maxwell postulate [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] on the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]: fields $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ jointly of class $C^1$ with the additional derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and continuous source densities $\rho,J$ of [[def-em-sources]]. Let $P,M$ and the derived objects $\rho_b,J_b,\rho_f,J_f,D,H$ be those of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]], with $P,M$ of class $C^2$, and use the operators of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. Then:

**(a) [Bound-source conservation]** $\partial_t\rho_b+\operatorname{div}J_b=0$ on $\Omega\times I$. Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the regular-distribution and classical-compatibility interfaces below. Identify continuous sources with their regular distributions using [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]] and [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]. Then

$$\partial_t\rho_f+\operatorname{div}J_f=\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J$$

as distributions on $U$, with derivatives as in [[def-distributional-derivative]]: the free pair is distributionally conserved exactly when the total pair is. Under the adopted four vacuum equations both sides are zero distributions, by [[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]]. These statements do not require classical derivatives of $\rho,J$. Where the partial derivatives $\partial_t\rho$ and $\partial_{x_i}J_i$ exist, the same identity holds pointwise by differentiating the free/bound decomposition; in particular, if these derivatives are continuous on $U$, both pairs satisfy the classical pointwise continuity equation. The bound-source conservation equation remains classical and uses only $P,M\in C^2$.

**(b) [Macroscopic equations]** On $\Omega\times I$,

$$\operatorname{div}D=\rho_f,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}H=J_f+\partial_tD.$$

**(c) [Interpretation and scope]** Equations (b) are an exact rewriting of the adopted vacuum equations under the decomposition of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]]: the two equations written in $E$ and $B$ are unchanged, and the $D$ and $H$ equations hold for every $C^2$ pair $(P,M)$, independently of any constitutive law. The classical bound identity of (a) uses the exchange of $\partial_t$ with $\operatorname{div}$ for $C^2$ data; the free/total identity is distributional in the stated continuous-source class, with its classical interpretation only under the additional derivatives stated in (a). The distributional conservation conclusion embeds the adopted smooth solution only; no macroscopic field-equation claim is made for the weak branch of the Maxwell postulate, for singular or sheet sources or for discontinuous $(P,M)$; no constitutive relation and no empirical statement is made.

**(b) [Elementary inertial-rest branch]** In the rest frame, with constant symmetric positive-definite matrices $\varepsilon,\mu\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ (the isotropic scalar cases $\varepsilon=\varepsilon\mathbf 1$, $\mu=\mu\mathbf 1$ with $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ included), the model takes

$$D=\varepsilon E,\qquad B=\mu H,\qquad J_c=\sigma E,$$

where $\sigma\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ is symmetric positive semidefinite and $J_c$ is the conduction part of the free current, $J_f=J_c+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ for a declared external free current $J_{\mathrm{ext}}:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ in $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. For a real matrix $T$, symmetric means $T^{\mathsf T}=T$, positive definite means $v^{\mathsf T}Tv>0$ for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^3$, and positive semidefinite means $v^{\mathsf T}Tv\ge0$ for every $v$. Entries of $\varepsilon,\mu,\sigma$ carry respectively $\mathrm F\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, $\mathrm H\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $\mathrm S\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, where $\mathrm F=\mathrm C/\mathrm V$, $\mathrm H=\mathrm T\,\mathrm m^2/\mathrm A$ and $\mathrm S=\mathrm A/\mathrm V$; these make the three displayed relations dimensionally consistent. Local, linear and nondispersive (instantaneous) response is part of this restricted assumption. In the isotropic case an exact broadband interpretation of the constant-coefficient law additionally requires $\varepsilon\mu\ge c^{-2}$, so that the characteristic speed $1/\sqrt{\varepsilon\mu}$ does not exceed the vacuum speed $c$; without that condition, and in the anisotropic branch, the constant-coefficient law is a declared finite-band effective phase-response model and carries no universal front-speed claim.

Let $e_z$ be a unit vector of $\mathbb R^3$ and identify $\mathbb R^3=\mathbb R^2\oplus\mathbb R e_z$ with transverse coordinates $(x_1,x_2)$; write $
abla_t h=(\partial_1h,\partial_2h)$, $\Delta_t h=\partial_1^2h+\partial_2^2h$ and, for a transverse $C^1$ map $u_t$ with components $(u_1,u_2)$, $\operatorname{div}_t u_t=\partial_1u_1+\partial_2u_2$ and $\operatorname{curl}_2 u_t=\partial_1u_2-\partial_2u_1$; regard $h$, $
abla_th$, $u_t$ and $e_z	imes u_t$ as $z$-independent fields on $\Omega_t	imes\mathbb R$, with $e_z$ the third basis vector. Let $h:\Omega_t	o\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ and $u_t:\Omega_t	o\mathbb R^2$ be $C^1$. Then, with the divergence, curl, cross product and inner product of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]:
(a) $\operatorname{div}(e_z	imes
abla_th)=0$; $\operatorname{curl}(e_z	imes
abla_th)=e_z\,\Delta_th$; $e_z	imes(e_z	imes
abla_th)=-
abla_th$; $
abla_th\cdot(e_z	imes
abla_th)=0$; $e_z\cdot(e_z	imes
abla_th)=0$; $|e_z	imes
abla_th|=|
abla_th|$;
(b) $\operatorname{curl}(e_zh)=-e_z	imes
abla_th$ and $\operatorname{div}(e_zh)=\partial_3h$ (which vanishes for $z$-independent $h$);
(c) $\operatorname{curl}(u_t)=e_z\operatorname{curl}_2u_t$, $\operatorname{div}(u_t)=\operatorname{div}_tu_t$, and $e_z	imes u_t$ is transverse.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].
For all $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$.

Every plane harmonic function is of class $C^\infty$ and is real analytic in the
two real coordinates.
If $f$ is $C^2$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, then $\partial_i\partial_j f=\partial_j\partial_i f$ for every pair of coordinate indices.

Let $n\ge2$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be bounded, nonempty and open. Two functions $u,v\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega)$ with $\Delta u=\Delta v$ in $\Omega$ and $u=v$ on $\partial\Omega$ agree on $\overline\Omega$. Thus prescribed classical Poisson equation and Dirichlet data have at most one such solution. Moreover, for equal Laplacians,
$$\sup_{\overline\Omega}|u-v|\le\sup_{\partial\Omega}|u-v|.$$
In particular, a sequence of such solutions with a common Laplacian and uniformly convergent boundary traces converges uniformly on the closure.

A nonempty open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is **star-shaped with respect to** $a\in U$ when

$$a+t(x-a)\in U\qquad\text{for every }x\in U\text{ and }0\le t\le1.$$

The point $a$ is a **star centre**. Every convex open set of [[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]] is star-shaped with respect to each of its points. The nonemptiness and the chosen centre are part of the definition.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. **Degenerate boxes.** If $a_i \le b_i$ are reals with $a_{i_0} = b_{i_0}$ for
   some $i_0 < n$, then every set $R$ between the open box
   $\{x : a_i < x_i < b_i\ (i<n)\}$ and the closed rectangle $[a,b]$ is Lebesgue
   measurable with $\lambda_n(R) = 0$.
2. **Coordinate hyperplanes.** For $i_0 < n$ and a real $c$, the set
   $$H_{i_0,c} \;:=\; \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : x_{i_0} = c \,\}$$
   is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(H_{i_0,c}) = 0$.

At $n = 1$ the hyperplane $H_{0,c}$ is the singleton $\{c\}$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Assume the elementary inertial-rest branch of [[post-em-material-closure]]: constant symmetric positive-definite matrices $\varepsilon,\mu\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ (isotropic scalar case included) with $D=\varepsilon E$ and $B=\mu H$, and the conduction relation $J_f=\sigma E+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ with $\sigma$ symmetric positive semidefinite and a declared external free current $J_{\mathrm{ext}}$. Assume the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with the regularity hypotheses of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]], so that its macroscopic equations hold on $\Omega\times I$. Define the stored-energy density and the energy-flux vector

$$u:=\tfrac12\bigl(E\cdot D+B\cdot H\bigr),\qquad S:=E\times H,$$

with the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]; $u$ carries $\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-1}\mathrm s^{-2}$ and $S$ carries $\mathrm W\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. Then:

**(a) [Local balance and positivity]** On $\Omega\times I$,

$$\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S=-J_f\cdot E.$$

Moreover $u=\tfrac12(E\cdot\varepsilon E+H\cdot\mu H)\ge0$, with $u(x,t)>0$ whenever $(E(x,t),H(x,t))\ne(0,0)$.

**(b) [Dissipation reading]** With $J_f=\sigma E+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ and $\sigma$ symmetric positive semidefinite, $E\cdot\sigma E\ge0$ and the balance reads

$$\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S+E\cdot\sigma E=-J_{\mathrm{ext}}\cdot E;$$

the nonnegative term $E\cdot\sigma E$ is the Ohmic dissipation density of the model.

**(c) [Fixed-volume balance]** Let $\Omega'\subseteq\Omega$ be open with $\overline{\Omega'}\subseteq\Omega$ carrying the finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation of [[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]], let $t_0<t_1$ with $(t_0,t_1)\subseteq I$, assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) as in that divergence theorem, and let $n$ be the outward unit normal of $\partial\Omega'$. Then for every $t\in(t_0,t_1)$,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega'}u(x,t)\,dx=-\int_{\Omega'}J_f\cdot E\,dx-\oint_{\partial\Omega'}S\cdot n\,dS.$$

**(d) [Scope]** The density $u=\tfrac12(E\cdot D+B\cdot H)$ is a stored-energy density only for this constant symmetric nondispersive model; for general dispersive, nonlocal, nonlinear or hysteretic response no instantaneous stored-energy density is defined or claimed by this item, and the general dispersive work balance is not supplied. The identities hold only where the fields and sources have the stated regularity, the fixed-volume form keeps its boundary term, and conservation of $\int_{\Omega\prime}u$ requires the sum of outward flux and volume work on the right of (c) to vanish, not merely zero boundary flux. No empirical claim is made.

[Potential form and the PEC boundary equivalence] Let $\varphi\in C^2(\overline A;\mathbb C)$ with $\Delta\varphi=0$, fix $\zeta\in\{+1,-1\}$, and put $	ilde E:=-
abla\varphi$, $ eta:=\zeta\omega/v$, $	ilde H:=\zeta e_z	imes	ilde E/Z$, with real fields $E=\operatorname{Re}(	ilde Ee^{i( eta x_3-\omega t)})$, $B=\mu\operatorname{Re}(	ilde He^{i( eta x_3-\omega t)})$. Then $	ilde E_3=0$ and $	ilde H_3=0$ because $e_z	imes	ilde E$ and $
abla\varphi$ are transverse [F2], so $E_z=B_z=0$ (TEM); and the four amplitude equations of [F1] hold: $\widehat{\operatorname{div}}(	ilde E)=-\Delta\varphi=0$; $\widehat{\operatorname{div}}(	ilde H)= rac{\zeta}{Z} igl(\partial_1(-	ilde E_2)+\partial_2(	ilde E_1) igr)=- rac{\zeta}{Z}\operatorname{curl}_2	ilde E=0$ because $	ilde E=-
abla\varphi$ has equal mixed partials [F3]; $\widehat{\operatorname{curl}}(	ilde E)=(i eta\partial_2\varphi,\ -i eta\partial_1\varphi,\ \operatorname{curl}_2	ilde E)=i eta e_z	imes	ilde E=i\omega\mu	ilde H$, using $	ilde H= rac{ eta}{\omega\mu}e_z	imes	ilde E$, which holds because $ rac{ eta}{\omega\mu}= rac{\zeta\omega/v}{\omega\mu}= rac{\zeta}{v\mu}= rac{\zeta}{Z}$ since $v\mu=\sqrt{\mu/\varepsilon}=Z$; and $\operatorname{curl}_2	ilde H=(\zeta/Z)\operatorname{div}_t	ilde E=0$, hence $\widehat{\operatorname{curl}}(	ilde H)=i eta e_z	imes	ilde H=i eta\, rac{\zeta}{Z}e_z	imes(e_z	imes	ilde E)=- rac{i\zeta eta}{Z}	ilde E=-i\omega\varepsilon	ilde E$ by [F2] and $ rac{\zeta eta}{Z}= rac{\omega/v}{Z}= rac{\omega}{vZ}=\omega\varepsilon$ because $vZ=1/\varepsilon$. Hence the real fields satisfy the source-free lossless macroscopic equations by [F1]. If the potential has a differentiable boundary trace on a smooth wall of $A$ with outward unit normal $n$ (an in-plane unit vector) and tangent $	au:=e_z	imes n$, then $n	imes	ilde E=(0,0,n_1	ilde E_2-n_2	ilde E_1)$ and, since $	ilde E=-
abla\varphi$, $n_1	ilde E_2-n_2	ilde E_1=n_2\partial_1\varphi-n_1\partial_2\varphi=-
abla\varphi\cdot	au=-\partial_	au\varphi$, so $n	imes	ilde E=-e_z\partial_	au\varphi$ (only the vanishing of this normal-cross field is used below); likewise $n\cdot	ilde H= rac{\zeta}{Z}n\cdot(e_z	imes	ilde E)= rac{\zeta}{Z}	ilde E\cdot(n	imes e_z)=- rac{\zeta}{Z}	ilde E\cdot	au= rac{\zeta}{Z}\partial_	au\varphi$ by the scalar triple product and $n	imes e_z=-	au$ [F2]. Since a separated real field vanishes identically exactly when its amplitude does [F1], the PEC conditions $n	imes E=0$ and $n\cdot B=0$ hold exactly when $\partial_	au\varphi=0$ along the wall. In a $C^1$ boundary parametrization the derivative of the potential trace is the parametrization speed times $\partial_	au\varphi$ (up to orientation); the chain rule and FTC [F6] therefore make it locally constant when PEC is imposed. A locally constant function on a connected boundary component is constant there, since any one of its value fibres and its complement are both relatively open.

[Converse classification and the star-shaped potential] Let $(\tilde E,\tilde H)$ be $C^1$ transverse amplitudes of a separated TEM field satisfying the four amplitude equations of [F1]. The third components of the two curl equations read $\operatorname{curl}_2\tilde E=i\omega\mu\tilde H_3=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}_2\tilde H=-i\omega\varepsilon\tilde E_3=0$, while the two divergence equations read $\operatorname{div}_t\tilde E=0$ and $\operatorname{div}_t\tilde H=0$ (the $i\beta$-terms vanish with the third components). The transverse part of Faraday reads $(0,0,0)$ in its third component and $(-i\beta\tilde E_2,\ i\beta\tilde E_1,0)=i\beta\,e_z\times\tilde E$ in its transverse components, so $i\beta\,e_z\times\tilde E=i\omega\mu\tilde H$ and, since $\omega\mu>0$, $\tilde H=\frac{\beta}{\omega\mu}e_z\times\tilde E$ with no division by $\beta$. Substituting into the transverse part of Ampere and using $e_z\times(e_z\times\tilde E)=-\tilde E$ [F2] gives $-i\frac{\beta^2}{\omega\mu}\tilde E=-i\omega\varepsilon\tilde E$, that is $(\beta^2-\varepsilon\mu\omega^2)\tilde E=0$. If $\tilde E\ne0$ then $\beta^2=\varepsilon\mu\omega^2$, so $\beta=\pm\omega/v$ by [F6]; if $\tilde E=0$ then Faraday gives $\tilde H=0$, and the zero field solves the equations for every longitudinal label $\beta$ with no dispersion conclusion. Finally, if $A$ is star-shaped and $\tilde E$ is a $C^1$ transverse closed field ($\operatorname{curl}_2\tilde E=0$), then its real and imaginary parts are closed $C^1$ fields on the star-shaped domain, so [F5] supplies $C^2$ potentials for each, hence a complex $\varphi\in C^2(A;\mathbb C)$ with $\tilde E=-\nabla\varphi$ after a sign change, and $\operatorname{div}_t\tilde E=0$ makes $\Delta\varphi=0$; no real-only or boundary-extension conclusion is inferred from interior exactness.

[Single-conductor obstruction] Suppose $\varphi\in C^2(\overline A;\mathbb C)$ is harmonic on the bounded connected domain $A$ and has constant boundary trace on each connected component of $\partial A$, with the PEC potential description of step 1.1 available. If $\partial A$ is connected, the trace is a single constant $c$, and applying [F4] to the real and imaginary parts of $\varphi$ and of the constant function $c$ gives $\varphi=c$ on $\overline A$; then $\tilde E=-\nabla\varphi=0$ and $\tilde H\propto e_z\times\tilde E=0$. For a rectangular cross-section with a potential in $C^2(A)\cap C(\overline A)$ having constant boundary trace the same argument applies, because [F4] requires only a bounded nonempty open set and no boundary regularity. For rectangular separated TEM amplitudes that are $C^1$ on the interior and continuous on the closure with the classical PEC traces on the open edges, fix a star centre $x_*$ and use the radial primitive $\psi(x)=\int_0^1\tilde E(x_*+t(x-x_*))\cdot(x-x_*)\,dt$ furnished by [F5]. It is $C^2$ on the interior with $\nabla\psi=\tilde E$; the displayed formula extends continuously to the closure by uniform continuity of the electric amplitude there. For two points on one open edge, apply the interior FTC line-integral identity on parallel interior segments and pass to the edge using this continuity. Thus the boundary potential increment is the integral of the continuous tangential electric trace, whose difference quotients give the edge derivative; PEC makes that derivative zero; by the one-variable constancy of [F6] the potential is constant on each open edge, and continuity at the corners joins those constants, so the trace is constant on $\partial A$ and [F4] gives $\psi$ constant, hence $\tilde E=0$ and $\tilde H=0$. Thus a single-conductor cross-section with connected boundary admits no nonzero TEM field in the stated potential form, and the same holds for the stated rectangular class.

[Coaxial annulus: potential and fields] In the annulus $A=\{a<|x|<b\}$ put $\varphi(x):=V\ln(b/|x|)/\ln(b/a)$ and choose the forward label $k:=\omega/v$ (so $\zeta=+1$). Since $\partial_i\ln|x|=x_i/|x|^2$ by [F6] and the chain rule, $\partial_i\partial_i\ln|x|=1/|x|^2-2x_i^2/|x|^4$ and $\Delta\ln|x|=2/|x|^2-2/|x|^2=0$, so $\Delta\varphi=0$ on $A$; also $\varphi=V$ on $|x|=a$ and $\varphi=0$ on $|x|=b$, so the trace is constant on each boundary circle. The constructed fields of step 1.1 are then $\tilde E=-\nabla\varphi=V e_r/(|x|\ln(b/a))$ with $e_r=x/|x|$, and $\tilde H=e_z\times\tilde E/Z=\bigl(V/(Z|x|\ln(b/a))\bigr)e_\varphi$ with $e_\varphi:=e_z\times e_r$; by step 1.1 they satisfy the source-free lossless macroscopic equations and the PEC conditions, and the longitudinal label satisfies $k=\omega/v$, nondispersive with no cutoff, so $k$ is real and nonzero for every $\omega>0$.

[Coaxial energies in polar coordinates] Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. With $W_e:=\frac12\varepsilon\int_A|\tilde E|^2dA$ and $W_m:=\frac12\mu\int_A|\tilde H|^2dA$, the polar formula of [F6] (Jacobian $r$; the omitted radial segment is null) and $|\tilde E|^2=Z^2|\tilde H|^2=V^2/(|x|^2\ln^2(b/a))$ give $\int_A|\tilde E|^2dA=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_a^b\frac{V^2}{r^2\ln^2(b/a)}r\,dr\,d\theta=\frac{2\pi V^2}{\ln(b/a)}$, using $\int_a^b dr/r=\ln(b/a)$ by [F6]. Hence $W_e=\frac12\varepsilon V^2\frac{2\pi}{\ln(b/a)}=\frac12CV^2$ with $C:=\frac{2\pi\varepsilon}{\ln(b/a)}$, and $W_m=\frac12\mu\frac{V^2}{Z^2}\frac{2\pi}{\ln(b/a)}=\frac12CV^2$ because $\mu/Z^2=\varepsilon$. On the inner wall the filling normal is $n=-e_r$, so the interface reading of [[def-em-guide-cavity-geometry]](b) gives $\tilde K_f=-n\times\tilde H=\tilde H_\varphi(a)e_z$. Integrating its axial amplitude around that circle gives $I=2\pi a\tilde H_\varphi(a)=2\pi V/(Z\ln(b/a))$. With $L:=\frac{\mu\ln(b/a)}{2\pi}$ one gets $\frac12LI^2=\frac12\frac{\mu\ln(b/a)}{2\pi}\frac{4\pi^2V^2}{Z^2\ln^2(b/a)}=\frac12\frac{2\pi\mu V^2}{Z^2\ln(b/a)}=\frac12CV^2=W_m$, and $LC=\frac{\mu\ln(b/a)}{2\pi}\frac{2\pi\varepsilon}{\ln(b/a)}=\varepsilon\mu$. The instantaneous per-length energies are $\frac12CV^2\cos^2\theta$ and $\frac12LI^2\cos^2\theta$ with $\theta=kx_3-\omega t$, by the definitions of $E$ and $B$ and the identity $\operatorname{Re}(we^{i\theta})^2+|{\operatorname{Im}}(we^{i\theta})|^2=|w|^2$; for $V=0$ all fields and energies vanish. For $V\ne0$ the two boundary components carry distinct constants $V$ and $0$, whereas $V=0$ gives the zero field with equal boundary constants; this respects the obstruction of step 2.1.

[Scope] Clause (a) is steps 1.1 and 1.2: the potential form gives TEM fields satisfying the equations and turns PEC on a smooth wall into the vanishing tangential potential derivative, the converse classification gives the two nonzero signs $\beta=\pm\omega/v$ and the unrestricted label for the zero field, and the star-shaped interior exactness is used only with the stated potential-trace hypotheses for boundary conclusions. Clause (b) is step 2.1, proved for the continuous-boundary harmonic-potential form and the stated rectangular class; the general reduction of an arbitrary TEM field to the potential form on a merely simply connected non-star-shaped cross-section is not asserted. Clause (c) is steps 2.2 and 3.1: the coaxial computation is conditional, in the declared lossless model, with the polar-measure branch the only place Countable Choice is used, and no lossy, radiation, empirical or signal-speed claim is made.

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, its SI units and its fields $E,B$ be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-si-conventions]] and [[def-em-fields]]. Fix $a,b>0$, write $x_t=(x_1,x_2)$, $e_z:=e_3$, and define $\nabla_t f=(\partial_1f,\partial_2f,0)$, $\Delta_t f=\partial_1^2f+\partial_2^2f$ and $\operatorname{div}_tu_t=\partial_1u_1+\partial_2u_2$ for the stated regularity, using [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]].
(a) [Straight guide] A straight guide region is $\Omega_A:=A\times\mathbb R$ where $A$ is either a bounded connected $C^1$ plane domain ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]) or the explicit rectangular cross-section; the rectangle has corners and is treated by its open faces, not asserted to be a $C^1$ boundary domain, with longitudinal axis $e_z$; for a rectangular cross-section $A=R_{ab}:=(0,a)\times(0,b)$ the region is called the rectangular guide and its walls are the four open faces $\{x_1=0\},\{x_1=a\},\{x_2=0\},\{x_2=b\}$. A rectangular cavity region is $\Omega_c:=(0,a)\times(0,b)\times(0,d)$ for fixed $d>0$, with the six open faces as its walls. The separate smooth-cavity spectral branch uses an explicitly declared bounded $C^\infty$ domain in $\mathbb R^3$ with its smooth PEC boundary; it is not the rectangular reflection class. Spatial derivatives are taken at fixed $t$; the fields are defined on $\Omega\times I$ with the regularity declared by each theorem.
(b) [PEC boundary model] On every open wall (a wall minus its edges) the ideal perfectly conducting boundary model declares the two conditions $n\times E=0$ and $n\cdot B=0$, where $n$ is the outward unit normal of that wall ($-e_1,+e_1,-e_2,+e_2$ on the four rectangular walls, and $\pm e_j$ on the six cavity walls). Its physical reading is the ideal-conductor limit of the stationary interface conditions of [[pthm-em-material-stationary-jumps]]: with $E=B=0$ inside the ideal conductor the tangential electric field and the normal magnetic field vanish, while the surface-charge and surface-current readings $\sigma_f=-n\cdot D$ and $K_f=-n\times H$ for the filling-side traces (the wall normal points from the filling into the conductor, so the jump is $0$ minus the filling trace) are determined by the traces and are not prescribed here. The supplier's hypotheses (a compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface with one-sided $C^1$ fields) cover a smooth stationary interface, not the $\sigma\to\infty$ idealization nor the box edges; the guide/cavity conditions on the open walls are therefore declared as an idealization of this definition, and no pointwise statement on the edges is made.
(c) [Zero-normal-B reflection class] For the rectangular box $Q=\prod_{j=1}^3(0,L_j)$ with $L=(a,b,d)$, the reflection class is the class of locally integrable fields $E,B$ on $Q$ whose extensions to the rectangular torus $\prod_j\mathbb R/(2L_j\mathbb Z)$, defined by extending $E_1$ evenly across the $x_1$-walls and oddly across the $x_2$-, $x_3$-walls and cyclically for $E_2,E_3$, and extending $B_1$ oddly across $x_1$ and evenly across $x_2,x_3$ and cyclically for $B_2,B_3$, are $L^2$ fields, together with the distributional constraints that $\operatorname{div}E$ and $\operatorname{div}B$ vanish on the torus for the extensions. This is the declared weak PEC model used for the cavity initial-value problem; when the reflected extensions are continuous across the walls, their odd components vanish there, giving $n\times E=0$ and $n\cdot B=0$ on the open walls. Smoothness only inside $Q$ does not imply this extension continuity. Initial data not in this class (for example data with trapped normal $B$) are excluded, as are the general $H(\operatorname{curl})$ boundary classes, which are defined by the mathematical suppliers and are not identified here with the classical conditions.
(d) [TE, TM, TEM] For a guide or cavity field $(E,B)$, the longitudinal components are $E_z:=E\cdot e_z$ and $B_z:=B\cdot e_z$; the field is called TE (transverse electric) if $E_z\equiv0$, TM (transverse magnetic) if $B_z\equiv0$, and TEM if both vanish, always relative to the named axis $e_z$.
(e) [Separated phasor convention] For $\omega>0$ and $\beta\in\mathbb C$, a $\beta$-$\omega$ separated phasor field on the guide is a real field of the form $F(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\tilde F(x_1,x_2)e^{i(\beta x_3-\omega t)}\bigr)$ with a complex amplitude $\tilde F$, componentwise; $\omega/(2\pi)$ is the frequency and $\beta$ the longitudinal propagation constant; when $\beta$ is real, $\beta>0$ describes propagation in the $+e_z$ direction under this phase convention, while a complex $\beta$ gives the spatial factor $e^{-\operatorname{Im}\beta x_3}$ and may grow in the opposite direction; each consuming branch states its selection.
(f) [Scope] The definition fixes the geometry, the PEC boundary model, the weak reflection class and the mode terminology; it asserts no field equation, no constitutive law and no existence or completeness of modes, Rectangular TE/TM candidates and the rectangular reflection class, declared smooth bounded PEC cavity spectral classes, and smooth straight-guide TEM potential branches (including the coaxial annulus) are within this geometry. No general non-rectangular TE/TM guide theory, circular-guide spectral classification, open-end or junction scattering, or arbitrary lossy model is supplied. The same stationary PEC geometry also hosts the explicitly declared constant scalar Ohmic cavity class and the full longitudinal finite-energy reflection class of the straight rectangular guide; constitutive and evolution claims belong to their consuming theorems, not this definition.

**Conventions fixed by this definition.** The definition records objects and conditions only: the guide and cavity regions, their open walls and outward normals, the ideal PEC boundary conditions with their interface reading and excluded idealization, the zero-normal-$B$ reflection class with its distributional divergence constraints, the axis-relative TE/TM/TEM terminology, and the separated phasor encoding of real fields. It asserts no field equation, no constitutive relation, no existence, uniqueness or completeness of modes, and no dissipation or energy claim; those belong to the consuming theorems, each of which restates the branch of the material model it uses. The rectangular cross-section is treated through its four open faces and is not asserted to be a $C^1$ boundary domain, and no pointwise condition on box edges is made.

Assume the elementary inertial-rest branch of [[post-em-material-closure]]: constant symmetric positive-definite matrices $\varepsilon,\mu\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ (isotropic scalar case included) with $D=\varepsilon E$ and $B=\mu H$, and the conduction relation $J_f=\sigma E+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ with $\sigma$ symmetric positive semidefinite and a declared external free current $J_{\mathrm{ext}}$. Assume the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with the regularity hypotheses of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]], so that its macroscopic equations hold on $\Omega\times I$. Define the stored-energy density and the energy-flux vector

$$u:=\tfrac12\bigl(E\cdot D+B\cdot H\bigr),\qquad S:=E\times H,$$

with the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]; $u$ carries $\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-1}\mathrm s^{-2}$ and $S$ carries $\mathrm W\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. Then:

**(a) [Local balance and positivity]** On $\Omega\times I$,

$$\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S=-J_f\cdot E.$$

Moreover $u=\tfrac12(E\cdot\varepsilon E+H\cdot\mu H)\ge0$, with $u(x,t)>0$ whenever $(E(x,t),H(x,t))\ne(0,0)$.

**(b) [Dissipation reading]** With $J_f=\sigma E+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ and $\sigma$ symmetric positive semidefinite, $E\cdot\sigma E\ge0$ and the balance reads

$$\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S+E\cdot\sigma E=-J_{\mathrm{ext}}\cdot E;$$

the nonnegative term $E\cdot\sigma E$ is the Ohmic dissipation density of the model.

**(c) [Fixed-volume balance]** Let $\Omega'\subseteq\Omega$ be open with $\overline{\Omega'}\subseteq\Omega$ carrying the finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation of [[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]], let $t_0<t_1$ with $(t_0,t_1)\subseteq I$, assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) as in that divergence theorem, and let $n$ be the outward unit normal of $\partial\Omega'$. Then for every $t\in(t_0,t_1)$,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega'}u(x,t)\,dx=-\int_{\Omega'}J_f\cdot E\,dx-\oint_{\partial\Omega'}S\cdot n\,dS.$$

**(d) [Scope]** The density $u=\tfrac12(E\cdot D+B\cdot H)$ is a stored-energy density only for this constant symmetric nondispersive model; for general dispersive, nonlocal, nonlinear or hysteretic response no instantaneous stored-energy density is defined or claimed by this item, and the general dispersive work balance is not supplied. The identities hold only where the fields and sources have the stated regularity, the fixed-volume form keeps its boundary term, and conservation of $\int_{\Omega\prime}u$ requires the sum of outward flux and volume work on the right of (c) to vanish, not merely zero boundary flux. No empirical claim is made.

Let $\omega>0$ and $T:=2\pi/\omega>0$.

**Scalar form.** Let $a,d\in\mathbb C$. Then

$$\frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}\bigl(ae^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\operatorname{Re}\bigl(de^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl(a\overline d\bigr).$$

**Vector forms.** Let $a,d\in\mathbb C^3$, write the same symbols for the componentwise complex-bilinear extensions of the Euclidean inner product and of the cross product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] to $\mathbb C^3$, and let $\operatorname{Re}$ act componentwise. In coordinate formulas, $\epsilon_{ijk}$ is $+1$ for even permutations of $(1,2,3)$, $-1$ for odd permutations and zero for repeated indices; all displayed repeated-index sums run from 1 to 3. Then

$$\frac1T\int_0^T\bigl\langle\operatorname{Re}\bigl(ae^{-i\omega t}\bigr),\operatorname{Re}\bigl(de^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\bigr\rangle\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\langle a,\overline d\rangle\bigr),\qquad \frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}\bigl(ae^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\times\operatorname{Re}\bigl(de^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl(a\times\overline d\bigr),$$

the integrals of the real vector-valued integrands being componentwise. The real-valued functions $\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t})$ are the time-dependent factors of the plane-wave fields of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]] at a fixed position, with the phase absorbed into $a$ and $d$; no electromagnetic interpretation is asserted. Real quadratic expressions may not be replaced by complex quadratic expressions without conjugation: the average is not $\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(ad)$ in general. For $a=d=1+i$ the proved average is $\tfrac12|1+i|^2=1$, whereas $\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}((1+i)^2)=0$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $\alpha \in
\mathbb{R}$. Suppose the limits of $f$ and of $g$ at $c$ exist, and write
$L := \lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ and $M := \lim_{x \to c} g(x)$
([[def-function-limit]]). Then:

1. the limit of $f + g$ at $c$ exists, and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} (f + g)(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} f(x) + \lim_{x \to c} g(x) \;=\; L + M ;$$
2. the limit of $\alpha f$ at $c$ exists, and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} (\alpha f)(x) \;=\; \alpha \lim_{x \to c} f(x) \;=\; \alpha L ;$$
3. the limit of $fg$ at $c$ exists, and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} (fg)(x) \;=\; \Bigl(\lim_{x \to c} f(x)\Bigr)\Bigl(\lim_{x \to c} g(x)\Bigr) \;=\; LM ;$$
4. if $M \ne 0$, then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the point
   $c$ is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient $f/g$ is defined on $A_0$ by
   $(f/g)(x) = f(x) / g(x)$, the limit of $(f/g)|_{A_0}$ at $c$ exists, and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} (f/g)|_{A_0}(x) \;=\; \frac{\lim_{x \to c} f(x)}{\lim_{x \to c} g(x)} \;=\; \frac{L}{M} .$$

Each equation asserts two things at once: that the limit on the left exists, and
that it has the stated value. Both are proved. The symbols denote by
[[lem-function-limit-unique]].

**Everything below is proved directly from $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$.** No
sequence is constructed and no choice principle is used, so all four claims are
theorems of ZF. Passing through
[[thm-sequential-criterion-for-function-limits]] instead would import the
countable choice spent in that theorem's converse direction, for no gain; see
[[rem-heine-criterion-choice-cost]].

**Why the quotient is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is simply not defined
where $g$ vanishes, and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ arbitrarily far from
$c$; restricting to $A_0$ is therefore forced. That this restriction still has
$c$ as a limit point, so that the limit there means anything at all, is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]]. The sequential analogue
[[thm-algebra-of-limits]] needs the corresponding hypothesis in the form "the
denominator sequence is nonzero at every index".

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

The branch function $\omega(\beta)=\sqrt{(\beta^2+k_c^2)/(\varepsilon\mu)}$ of [F4] is differentiable with $v_g:=\omega'(\beta)=\frac{\beta}{\varepsilon\mu\omega(\beta)}$: indeed for real $h\ne0$ the difference quotient is $\frac{2\beta+h}{\varepsilon\mu(\omega(\beta+h)+\omega(\beta))}$ (rationalizing the difference of square roots), and its limit as $h\to0$ is $\frac{2\beta}{2\varepsilon\mu\omega(\beta)}$ by [F4]; differentiating the identity $\varepsilon\mu\omega(\beta)^2=\beta^2+k_c^2$ with the chain rule gives the same value.
